articles.title: Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure: Definitions, Management, Prognostication, and Transplantation.
articles.abstract: Acute-on-chronic liver failure is a rapidly evolving syndrome characterized by acute decompensation, organ failure, and high short-term mortality. This article reviews international definitions, epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnostic evaluation, critical-care management, prognostic models, liver transplantation (LT), posttransplant risk assessment, palliative care, current controversies, and emerging research. The recommended clinical approach emphasizes prompt identification of reversible precipitants, evidence-based organ support, serial assessment of disease trajectory during the first week, early referral for LT evaluation when appropriate, and alignment of treatment intensity with prognosis and patient preferences.
articles.authors: Yagan Lina, Mohan Rahul, Hernaez Ruben

articles.title: Critical Care Management of Disaster-Related Organ Failure.
articles.abstract: Disasters generate high volumes of multisystem trauma while simultaneously degrading the staff, equipment, and electricity that critical care depends on. This article reviews management of disaster-related organ failure under resource constraint. It outlines step-wise respiratory support, from high-flow nasal cannula and noninvasive ventilation to lung-protective mechanical ventilation; prevention and treatment of acute kidney injury (AKI), including dialysis options for AKI and end-stage renal disease patients; recognition of hemorrhagic, neurogenic, cardiogenic, and obstructive shock; and secondary complications including coagulopathy, hypothermia, abdominal compartment syndrome, hepatic dysfunction, and hyperglycemia. Ethical triage, palliation, telecritical care, and staffing models are also addressed.
articles.source: The Surgical clinics of North America
articles.authors: Hertel Kristie, Bard Michael

articles.title: Rehabilitation in the Intensive Care Unit: Preparing Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Professionals to Support Biopsychosocial Well-Being.
articles.abstract: With medical advances, more critically ill patients survive and often experience new or worsening physical, cognitive, and/or mental health sequelae. The intensive care unit involves interdisciplinary survival-focused care, and its biopsychosocial impact is profound and long-lasting. In this article, we have highlighted the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning as a person-centered, holistic, and contextually grounded framework for early rehabilitation specifically for critical care survivorship. The goal of this article is to elucidate the key role of physical medicine and rehabilitation professionals in enhancing the recovery trajectory of critical illness survivors within a transdiagnostic, interdisciplinary framework.
articles.source: Physical medicine and rehabilitation clinics of North America
articles.authors: Merbitz Nancy, Hampton Jessica M, Mladen Samantha N, et al.

articles.title: Mobilizing the Critically Ill: The Central Role of Nurses in Preventing ICU Complications and Enhancing Recovery.
articles.abstract: The intensive care unit (ICU) is a high-acuity environment where patients with severe illness receive comprehensive care. Immobility is common among patients with critical disease states and contributes to muscle atrophy, development of pressure ulcers, increased risk of thromboembolic events, and acute respiratory insufficiency. Similarly, delirium is another prevalent complication that further contributes to prolonged ICU stays, increased mortality, and long-term cognitive impairments. Reduced mobility, delirium, and other sequelae of critical illness pose significant challenges to patient recovery and often result in poor long-term outcomes. Early mobility has been shown to improve long-term outcomes of critically ill patients by reducing their length of hospital and ICU stay, reducing ICU-acquired weakness, improving functional outcomes, and improving long-term cognitive function. Given their direct patient contact, nurses are uniquely positioned to serve as the primary facilitators of patient mobility in the ICU. articles.authors: Patel Dhaval, DuMont Tiffany, Kuniak Lindsay, et al.

articles.title: Intraosseous Vascular Access.
articles.abstract: Intraosseous (IO) vascular access is a high-yield bedside procedure for adult inpatient and critical care medicine. When deployed early in high-acuity situations, IO access provides rapid, reliable central vascular access with high success rates and very rare major complications. Effective use requires appropriate site and needle selection, multimodal confirmation of appropriate placement, and vigilant monitoring for extravasation and neurovascular compromise. In awake patients, analgesia, including consideration of IO lidocaine before the initial flush, improves tolerance. IO-derived laboratory results can be useful when no alternative access exists but should be treated as provisional and confirmed once definitive access is secured.
articles.source: The Medical clinics of North America
articles.authors: Voronina Angelina, Freidinger Alexander G, Lords Allie, et al.

articles.title: Prediction, Prescription, and Proactive Medication Management in the Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: This narrative review examines the evolving role of prediction analytics in comprehensive medication management for critically ill patients. Intensive care unit pharmacotherapy is challenged by medication complexity, physiologic instability, heterogeneous treatment response, and continuous data streams. Predictive systems may support proactive medication management by identifying medication-related harm, therapeutic failure, optimization opportunities, and pharmacist workload earlier in the patient trajectory. The review discusses medication-informed prediction models, prescriptive analytics, workload-aware critical care pharmacist allocation, and potential future applications. Implementation requires actionable predictions, workflow integration, clinician oversight, and attention to equity, safety, and model credibility.
articles.authors: Murray Brian

articles.title: Intensive Monitoring, Big Data, and Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care.
articles.abstract: Intensive care is defined by providing a higher level of patient monitoring, but only a fraction of the data created through continuous hemodynamic monitoring are captured in the electronic health record. The monitoring data that is captured misses clinically important deterioration events and is not adequate to represent critical illness physiology for care at the bedside or for research. This article describes the current state of patient monitoring in intensive care, advanced monitors in development, metadata and its role in creating rich intensive care data sources, and machine learning and its current and future applications in intensive care medicine.
articles.authors: Rzewnicki Daniel I, Bhavani Sivasubramanium V

articles.title: Redesigning Intensive Care Unit Workflows: A Learning Health System Approach to Improving Care Delivery.
articles.abstract: Critical care leaders are increasingly asked to improve outcomes, reduce burden, and implement evidence-based care in complex, highly interdependent clinical environments. Meeting this challenge requires redesigning the workflows through which care is delivered, not simply measuring outcomes or adding new tools. This article presents a learning health system model that integrates sociotechnical systems thinking, quality improvement, health services research, and informatics to support workflow redesign. Multidimensional workflow signals inform the Diagnose, Redesign, Implement, Verify, Evolve (DRIVE) cycle to make care delivery more reliable, less burdensome, and better aligned with outcomes that matter to patients.
articles.authors: Murphy David J

articles.title: Optimizing Team Integration of Critical Care Pharmacists: Where We Go Next.
articles.abstract: Critical care pharmacists (CCPs) are essential members of the intensive care unit team who provide comprehensive medication management to improve patient outcomes, safety, and cost efficiency. This article highlights barriers to optimal integration of CCPs within multidisciplinary teams as well as opportunities to address them. Persistent barriers include financial, workforce, data, interprofessional, and regulatory. Strategies to address these gaps may involve standardized metrics, innovative staffing models, and research to strengthen evidence-based implementation. Metrics should include all members of the Stakeholder Triad and should include a mix of workload metrics, safety and efficacy metrics, and work-design metrics.
articles.authors: Smith Susan E, Henry Kelli, Papadopoulos John, et al.

articles.title: Optimizing Team Integration of Critical Care Pharmacists: A History of Critical Care Pharmacy Practice and Evolving Definition of "Optimal Practice".
articles.abstract: Critical Care Pharmacists (CCPs) are essential members of the intensive care unit (ICU) team who provide comprehensive medication management to improve patient outcomes, safety, and cost efficiency. This article highlights best practices for optimal CCP integration, including optimal patient-to-pharmacist ratios, participation in interprofessional rounds, team-based practice models, and expanded coverage across all shifts. The Triple Domain framework is useful to evaluate CCP value across patients, health care teams, and institutions. Best practices include an ICU patient-to-CCP ratio of less than or equal to 15:1 and inclusion of CCPs on daily interprofessional rounds.
articles.authors: Smith Susan E, Bektas Aeryana N, Henry Kelli, et al.

articles.title: The COVID-19 Pandemic as a Stress Test of the Intensive Care Unit Workforce.
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic monumentally strained the intensive care unit (ICU) workforce and revealed both the strengths and vulnerabilities in contemporary critical care delivery. In this review, we briefly describe the composition of the US ICU workforce and the organizational features most relevant to staffing. Next, we examine how the pandemic disrupted critical care delivery, specifically health care workers. Finally, we discuss the lasting psychological toll and workforce attrition; highlight adaptations that emerged, such as tele-ICU expansion, virtual family engagement, tiered staffing models, rapid-onboarding curricula, and peer support programs; and outline priorities for policy, practice, and research to strengthen workforce resilience.
articles.authors: Connell Kathryn A, Vranas Kelly C, Yu Hyunmin, et al.

articles.title: The Intensive Care Unit Team: Roles, Scope, and Interprofessional Interdependence in the Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: A hallmark feature of an intensive care unit (ICU) is the presence of a structured team-based interprofessional model. Although composition of the ICU team varies by organization and patient population, it typically includes critical care nurses, intensivists, respiratory therapists, and clinical pharmacists. Interprofessional teams in ICUs are associated with increased collaboration and improved patient outcomes. However, the ICU team faces challenges in workforce shortages, staffing gaps, and ineffective information sharing, which can inhibit effective team function. Proven strategies to support collaboration among the ICU team include structured interprofessional rounds, strong leadership of the team, care protocols, and quality bundles.
articles.authors: Manzo Laura L, Christoph Ella N I, Kessinger Stephanie K, et al.

articles.title: External hydrocephalus in adult neurocritical patients.
articles.abstract: External hydrocephalus (EH) in adults is an underrecognized clinical entity characterized by CSF circulatory failure and progressive subarachnoid space (SAS) dilation under high intracranial pressure (ICP). Data regarding its incidence, pathophysiology, and management in adult neurocritical care are sparse. To describe the incidence, risk factors and outcome of EH in adult neurocritical patients. Prospective study of patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (msTBI) or spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) admitted to intensive care unit (ICU). Three subgroups ere defined: 1) radiological EH: dilated SAS between two successive CT scans; 2) radiological EH in the context of intracranial hypertension (IH): suspected o confirmed elevated ICP; and 3) radiological EH and invasively documented elevated ICP. A total of 128 patients were included (78 msTBI, 50 SAH). The incidence of radiological EH was 20.3 % (26.9 % in msTBI and 10 % in SAH), while the incidence of radiological EH in the context of IH was 7.8 % (10.3 % in msTBI vs. 4 % in SAH). articles.title: Streamlining the Evidence-to-Practice Pathway With Computerised Decision Support in Anaesthesiology and Critical Care: A Qualitative Study of Clinician and System-Level Interest Holder Perspectives Across Five Scandinavian Countries.
articles.abstract: Implementing evidence-based recommendations in anaesthesiology and critical care remains challenging due to guideline, workflow and contextual barriers. Guideline-based computerised clinical decision support systems (CDSS), embedded in structured pathways linking international guidelines to Scandinavian-endorsed recommendations and delivered via electronic health records, may help strengthen the evidence-to-practice pathway. This study aimed to explore perceived barriers and facilitators to their use. This qualitative study interviewed 10 clinicians (anaesthesiologists and intensivists; specialists and non-specialists; < 40 and ≥ 40 years; male and female) and nine system-level stakeholders (hospital and health authority representatives) from Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. We integrated endorsed international guidelines into a CDSS providing patient-specific reminders linked to recommendations, as well as shared decision-making tools and decision-analytic components. Using a simulation application, participants explored the CDSS in a demo electronic health record. articles.title: A Survey of Clinician-Reported Management of Hypernatremia in the ICU.
articles.abstract: Hypernatremia is frequent in the intensive care unit (ICU) and is associated with adverse outcomes. Despite its prevalence, robust evidence to guide treatment is lacking, and global practice patterns are largely unknown. We investigated global treatment preferences and clinicians' willingness to enroll patients in a randomized trial to inform its feasibility. This international cross-sectional online survey comprised 20 primarily closed-ended questions, using five-point Likert-scale responses, across four themes: treatment method, threshold, correction rate, and opinion on a proposed trial. Respondents considered a clinical vignette of hypernatremia developing before or during ICU admission, excluding dehydration and chronic causes. It was distributed to ICU physicians worldwide. The survey was sent to 3053 ICU physicians in 17 countries, with 1051 respondents, yielding a response rate of 34%. Of respondents, 74% were consultants, and 26% were residents. articles.title: Serious Adverse Events in Adult ICU Patients: A Substudy of the PATIENCE Cohort.
articles.abstract: Prokinetic agents are used to enhance upper gastrointestinal motility, but adverse events related to these agents are poorly described. We aimed to provide detailed epidemiological data on predefined serious adverse events (SAEs) in a cohort of adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients with and without prokinetic treatment. We hypothesised that all predefined SAEs would occur in both patients treated and those not treated with prokinetic agents, and that a higher number of SAEs would occur among patients treated with prokinetic agents for more than three consecutive days. This substudy of the inception cohort study "Prokinetic agents in adult intensive care unit patients" included acutely admitted adult ICU patients. The prokinetic agents assessed (exposures) were erythromycin, metoclopramide, domperidone, and prucalopride. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients experiencing at least one episode of five pre-specified SAEs during ICU stay (cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, vomiting with aspiration, diarrhoea, extrapyramidal symptoms). articles.title: Discussing Future Treatment and Care in the ICU: Perspectives From Patients.
articles.abstract: Treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) is usually predicated on curative treatment, but continuing all available treatment options may not always be beneficial for the patient or in line with their wishes. However, patients admitted to the ICU are often assessed as incapable of making decisions regarding their care; hence conversations about wishes for treatment are postponed. This study aimed to investigate the experiences of patients who participated in a conversation concerning treatment and care following ICU discharge based on the Danish version of the Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment (ReSPECT) form. Semi-structured telephone interviews were conducted with patients who had a conversation about future treatment and care with an intensivist using the ReSPECT form during an ICU admission between November 2024 and July 2025. Relatives who participated in the conversation and were present during the interviews were asked to elaborate on their experiences of the conversation's timing and how they felt about participating in the conversation. articles.title: Swedish Consensus Recommendation for Follow-Up After ICU Stay.
articles.abstract: A substantial proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) survivors experience long-term physical, psychological and cognitive impairments after critical illness. However, methods for identifying patients in need of post-ICU support vary widely. As a result, many patients are left without access to established rehabilitation pathways. This consensus recommendation provides a framework for the organisation and content of follow-up for adult ICU survivors in Sweden, informed by available evidence, stakeholder perspectives and expert consensus. The National System for Knowledge-Driven Healthcare Management (NPO) in Sweden commissioned the development of a practice recommendation for the follow-up of critically ill adults. Multidisciplinary experts in ICU survivorship formed a task force group. A systematic literature search in four databases was conducted in 2024 to identify pre-existing systematic reviews on the topic. The literature was reviewed, assessed for quality and recommendations were developed based on the literature evidence. articles.title: Pressure injury prevention in critical care: A reflexive thematic analysis of clinicians' perspectives on complexity and clinical judgement.
articles.abstract: Pressure injury prevention in critical care remains a persistent global challenge. Despite established guidelines, implementation is often constrained by physiological instability, device burden, and competing clinical priorities. Emerging digital and artificial intelligence approaches offer potential support, yet their role within the complexity of critical care practice remains unclear. To explore clinicians' perspectives on pressure injury prevention in critical care, with particular attention to complexity, clinical decision-making and the potential role of emerging technologies. Qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis. We analysed 12 brief written reflections from clinicians working in critical care and related roles, predominantly in the United Kingdom. We purposively invited contributors through professional networks, who responded to shared prompts on prevention challenges, practice tensions, and potential roles for artificial intelligence. articles.title: Metabolic dysfunction in chronic critical illness: mechanisms, clinical consequences and therapeutic perspectives.
articles.abstract: Advances in intensive care have improved survival from acute critical illness, leading to a growing population of patients with chronic critical illness (CCI), many of whom require prolonged organ support. This condition is associated with persistent catabolism, inflammation, and poor long-term outcomes. Understanding the metabolic alterations underlying this failure to recover may help identify targets for monitoring and intervention. This review synthesizes current clinical and translational evidence on metabolic dysregulation in CCI and discusses its implications for monitoring, nutritional strategies, and therapeutic interventions. We performed a narrative review informed by a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE followed by manual reference screening. Preclinical, translational and clinical studies addressing energy metabolism, mitochondrial function, autophagy, ketone metabolism, inflammation and recovery trajectories in critical illness were qualitatively synthesized. articles.title: How are researchers using MIMIC? A sampling-based methods review.
articles.abstract: The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) database is a widely used open data resource in critical care research. Its accessibility has led to large numbers of research studies being published; however, design and analysis decisions made by individual studies may vary, affecting comparability and reproducibility. We conducted a sampling-based methods review of research that analysed the MIMIC database. Studies published between 2015 and 2025 were eligible for inclusion in the sampling frame. A random sample of 100 eligible studies was identified through the OpenAlex bibliographic database; data were collected using a structured extraction framework. Information was extracted on study aims, cohort definitions, exclusion criteria, outcome specification, handling of missing data, and analytical methods. The review focused on how key design and analytical decisions were reported and justified in the random sample. Studies reported findings from general ICU and specific clinical populations; the study population could not be determined for 32 of the 100 studies. articles.title: Analysis of work system components in interprofessional communication to determine shock etiology.
articles.abstract: In critical care settings, lack of agreement among clinicians on shock etiology is associated with higher mortality. Effective interprofessional communication may facilitate agreement on etiology and reduce mortality. This study sought to understand the interaction of work system components (people, environments, tools, tasks) in interprofessional communication to determine shock etiology. We interviewed 28 physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses, and pharmacists at three United States hospitals using a Critical Incident Technique. Analysis was guided by the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety model. The principal finding was that clinicians worked across fragmented physical, socio-organizational, and digital environments to balance the urgency to treat shock with intermediate steps to reduce diagnostic uncertainty. The results suggest that future research should acknowledge the benefits of productive disagreement among clinicians and develop supports that promote synchronous communication by bridging physical and socio-organizational fragmentation, compiling and systematizing relevant clinical information, and generating shared awareness among clinicians.

articles.title: Training of trainers on medical education reforms: a prospective multicenter French survey among intensivists.
articles.abstract: The recent reform of the second cycle of medical education in France introduced competency-based medical education (CBME) with the incorporation of several pedagogical modalities into undergraduate training and assessment, including objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs), simulation-based teaching (SBT), and clinical reasoning (CR) instruction throughout the academic year. While these tools are central to preparing competent practitioners, their effective implementation depends on adequately trained educators. We hypothesized that training would be insufficient, notably in the recently introduced pedagogical modalities. We conducted a national, cross-sectional survey (June-September 2023) to assess the level and adequacy of training of board-certified physicians practicing in critical care and involved in undergraduate teaching. An anonymous online questionnaire collected demographic data, teaching frequency, training characteristics, perceived adequacy and usefulness of training, preparedness, and barriers. articles.title: Beyond the ICU: family resilience and emotional turmoil after intensive care - a qualitative study.
articles.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, visitation restrictions in ICUs intensified psychological distress among family members, yet the long-term impact of psychosocial support on family resilience remains poorly understood. To evaluate the experiences of family members during the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on interactions with healthcare professionals and well-being 18th months after hospitalisation. A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured interviews with 14 families of patients admitted to the ICU in spring 2020.Data were analysed using inductive content analysis. Experiences were shaped by caring interactions with healthcare professionals, emotional disruption, and reliance on family support. Clear information and psychosocial support fostered trust but were also associated with stress and feelings of isolation. articles.title: Effect of Spatial Distance From the Crash Scene to a Critical Care Center on Traffic Fatality Rates in Japan.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the association between spatial distance from the traffic-crash scene to the nearest critical care center and traffic-crash fatality in Japan. Fatality rate rose approximately linearly with distance: 0.50% (< 5 km), 0.92% (5-15 km), and 2.29% (≥ 15 km), a 7.1-fold increase beyond 30 km versus the 0-1 km band. Crashes < 5 km were predominantly intersection- and pedestrian-related, whereas crashes ≥ 15 km were disproportionately single-lane, straight-road and single-vehicle events. articles.title: Clinical application of volatile sedation in adult intensive care units: pharmacological mechanisms, delivery systems, and safety.
articles.abstract: Sedation is essential in critically ill mechanically ventilated patients, yet conventional intravenous agents carry risks of accumulation, organ-dependent clearance, and adverse effects. Volatile anesthetics offer several pharmacokinetic advantages, but their adoption in the intensive care unit has historically been limited by technical constraints. This review offers an updated, clinically focused overview of volatile-based sedation in adult intensive care units, covering pharmacological mechanisms, delivery systems, clinical outcomes, safety, and practical application. This review was conducted through systematic searching of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between January 2016 and December 2025. Sevoflurane and isoflurane achieve sedation primarily via γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor modulation and offer organ-independent clearance, rapid onset/offset, and real-time end-tidal monitoring. Modern delivery systems, including reflection devices (Sedaconda-ACD) and automated platforms (MIRUS), have improved intensive care unit feasibility. articles.title: Burn Management in Disasters.
articles.abstract: Burn disasters are uncommon but uniquely resource-intensive mass casualty events, requiring prolonged multidisciplinary care that can rapidly exhaust the limited number of verified burn centers and beds. This article reviews the epidemiology and injury patterns of burn disasters, burn-specific triage and transport principles, and system-level planning built on regional burn networks. It examines the American Burn Association's role in center verification, regional response plans, and national burn bed capacity monitoring, alongside federal support mechanisms. Acute resuscitation, damage-control operative strategies, temporary wound coverage, workforce augmentation, and pediatric considerations are addressed, together with ethical decision-making, long-term recovery, and emerging technologies.

articles.title: Weekly Multidisciplinary Intensive Care Unit Debriefings Provide Effective Support for Intensive Care Unit Nurses.
articles.abstract: Nursing burnout is a rising crisis, characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and a diminished sense of accomplishment. Primary drivers include chronic staffing shortages, high-intensity workloads, interpersonal conflict, and inadequate resources to tackle work-related issues. In 2016, we launched daily multidisciplinary debriefings to mitigate the effects of such issues in our 18-bed intensive care unit (ICU). It was very effective, but daily meetings were perceived to be burdensome from a workload perspective. Safety restrictions during the coronavirus disease (2019-2020) pandemic and logistical challenges thereafter forced a suspension of debriefing meetings. To address continued needs, we resumed these operational debriefings in June 2025, electing to hold them on a weekly rather than daily basis. To assess the efficacy and impact of weekly multidisciplinary operational debriefings on ICU staff. articles.title: Patient- and Family-centred Nursing Communication in the Intensive Care Unit: A Bibliometric Analysis.
articles.abstract: As a fundamental component of critical care, patient- and family-centred nursing communication in the intensive care unit is not merely an information exchange process, but a professional behaviour that requires practical skills. This study aims to employ bibliometric analysis to elucidate the prevailing research focal points and trends within patient- and family-centred nursing communication. Relevant articles were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. CiteSpace and VOSviewer were used for bibliometric analysis and visualization of countries, institutions, authors, and keywords. From 2006 to 2025, annual publications showed a fluctuating upward trend. A total of 925 publications were included, authored by 4048 authors from 1651 institutions. Research hotspots included the impact of communication, communication management, and context-specific communication. articles.title: Development and Pilot Psychometric Testing of the ICU-HQI to Assess Handover Quality in Intensive Care Units.
articles.abstract: Effective information handover during shift changes is critical for patient safety in intensive care units (ICUs). Despite extensive research on handover practices, measurement instruments with preliminary psychometric evidence applicable across different nursing roles and ICU contexts remain limited. To develop and conduct a preliminary psychometric evaluation of the ICU-HQI questionnaire for assessing ICU nursing professionals' perceptions of handover quality. A pilot cross-sectional methodological study was conducted in 2 ICUs with different physical layouts (open-box and closed-box) in a tertiary hospital in Spain. Content validity was assessed through a Delphi process. The questionnaire was administered to nursing staff, and exploratory dimensionality analysis using principal components analysis was performed to examine the internal structure of the instrument and its internal consistency. articles.title: Effect of Chlorhexidine Oral Care on Ventilator-Associated Events in 4 ICU Populations: A Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract: Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) oral care is used to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia, but its effectiveness in reducing ventilator-associated events (VAE) remains unclear. VAE encompasses both infectious and noninfectious complications. To examine the impact of twice daily 0.12% CHG oral care on VAE, length of stay (LOS), mechanical ventilator (MV) hours, and in-hospital mortality in 4 intensive care unit (ICU) populations: cardiac surgical, cardiac medical, multisystem, and neurological. An analysis using an electronic health record clinical database of 1567 mechanically ventilated patients from a quaternary hospital in central Florida was conducted. χ2, ANOVA, logistic regression, linear regression, and mediation analysis using LOS and MV hours as mediators assessed the relationship between CHG oral care and clinical outcomes. The cardiac surgical population had the highest VAE rate (47.13), whereas the neurological ICU had the lowest (5.87) per 1000 ventilator days. articles.title: Say No to Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections: A Sustained Quality Improvement Initiative in the Neuro Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: In 2022 and 2023, the Neuroscience Intensive Care Unit (ICU) reported 12 catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs), a marked increase from previous years, prompting a comprehensive review of catheter use, current urine culture collection practices, and evidence-based practices. The aim of this quality improvement (QI) project was to address gaps in urine culture collection technique, reduce excessive catheter days, foster a unit culture that prioritized evidence-based urinary catheter management, and reduce CAUTI rates over a 3-year period. A multidisciplinary initiative was launched, involving staff education, protocol development, and process changes. Key interventions included direct education sessions on proper urine culture collection, implementation of the Neuroscience ICU Urinary Protocol, the Urinary Catheter Nurse-Driven Removal Protocol, and the Urinalysis (UA) and Urine Culture Collection Protocol. PED is associated with negative patient outcomes, both short and long term. This study investigated the prevalence of PED and its potential risk factors, as well as the prevalence of voice impairment and laryngeal injuries and their associations with dysphagia. This is a prospective study of adult ICU patients intubated for more than 48 h. Flexible Endoscopic Evaluation of Swallowing (FEES) was conducted bedside on all patients, by nine trained speech and language pathologists (SLP), following a standard protocol assessing function and structure of the velopharynx, pharynx, larynx, voice, and swallowing function. Dysphagia evaluation and ratings coincided during FEES, while voice and laryngeal injuries were retrospectively rated from FEES recordings. articles.abstract: Maintaining endotracheal tube cuff pressure (20-30 cmH2O) is vital to prevent aspiration and tracheal injury. While manometry is considered the gold standard for monitoring cuff pressure, clinical adherence remains suboptimal among critical care providers, including intensive care unit (ICU) nurses and respiratory therapists, leading to potential patient safety risks. Therefore, this study investigated factors influencing critical care providers' intention to use a manometer, based on the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). This cross-sectional study was conducted in 2024 among 186 ICU nurses working in four public hospitals in Amol, Iran. Nurses were enrolled through census sampling. Data were collected using a demographic checklist, a checklist of ICU ward structural characteristics, and a validated TPB-based scale assessing attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and intention. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and multiple linear regression. The mean (standard deviation) score of intention to use a manometer was 17.81 (3.97). articles.abstract: Reduce lines, drains, airways (LDA) dislodgements by 50% in 6 months, as tracked by situation, background, assessment, recommendation dislodgement forms, and safety incident reports. LDA dislodgement is a significant safety concern leading to extended hospital stays, increased costs, and poorer patient outcomes. From January to May 2024, the SICU experienced 31 LDA dislodgements. The LDA Taskforce, consisting of nursing staff and leadership, implemented several strategies. Door signage categorized patients by risk level, and an in-service binder was developed to educate staff using the "teach-back" method. Key methods included appropriate restraint usage, 2 registered nurse handoffs during transitions, a "time-out" before patient movement, and proper LDA securement. Post-incident debriefings helped identify and address gaps. Data on dislodgements were collected weekly. Before the project, there were 31 dislodgements from January to May 2024. articles.title: Relationship Between Level of Consciousness, Pressure Ulcer Risk, and Pain Behaviors in Mechanically Ventilated Patients.
articles.abstract: Mechanically ventilated patients are vulnerable to pain, pressure injuries, and decreased levels of consciousness. This descriptive and correlational study examined the relationship between the level of consciousness, pressure injury risk, and pain behaviors in 150 patients treated in the intensive care units of a university hospital between November 2023 and February 2024. Data were collected using the Behavioral Pain Scale (BPS), Jackson/Cubbin Pressure Area Risk Assessment Tool, and Full Outline of UnResponsiveness (FOUR) Score. The mean FOUR Score was 6.78 ± 2.15, the mean Jackson/Cubbin score was 29.68 ± 2.79, and the mean BPS score was 4.73 ± 1.46. Pressure injury risk was significantly related to inotropic support and skin integrity (P < .001). Patients receiving enteral nutrition and those without sedation or inotropic support had higher BPS scores (P < .05). Weak positive correlations were found between the FOUR Score and both BPS (r = 0.190) and Jackson/Cubbin scores (r = 0.306). articles.title: Exploration of Professional Competence and Moral Sensitivity in Critical Care Unit Nurses.
articles.abstract: Nursing competence is a key aspect of health care quality. This study aimed to explore the relationship between professional competence and moral sensitivity in nurses working in critical care units, utilizing a cross-sectional design. The study was conducted in 2018 and included nurses working in critical care units who met the inclusion criteria of having at least 1 year of experience in cardiac care units and holding a bachelor's degree. Data were collected through a demographic questionnaire, the Competency Inventory for Registered Nurses, and the Moral Sensitivity Questionnaire. The findings revealed a weak positive correlation between professional competence and moral sensitivity (r = 0.319, P = .002). Age, number of shifts, and type of hospital were also significantly correlated with nurses' professional competence and moral sensitivity. Given the direct correlation between professional competence and moral sensitivity, as well as the factors influencing these variables, it is recommended that nursing managers focus on developing programs to enhance them. articles.title: Impact of Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE II) Scores on the Occurrence of a Hospital-Acquired Pressure Injury in ICU Patients: A Comparative Analytical Study.
articles.abstract: Pressure injuries represent a significant challenge for patients, healthcare professionals, and health systems. Their incidence serves as an indicator of quality of care in both primary and specialized care settings. To determine the association between Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE II) scores and the development of hospital-acquired pressure injuries in ICU patients. A retrospective cohort study with comparative analysis was conducted. Critically ill patients admitted to a tertiary care hospital between July 2022 and January 2023 were categorized into two groups based on the presence or absence of pressure injuries. The Braden score was assessed for each patient, and APACHE II scores were stratified into four groups: group 1 (scores 31-40), group 2 (scores 21-30), group 3 (scores 11-20), and group 4 (scores 3-10). Pressure injuries occurred in 46% of patients. Patients with pressure injuries had a mean APACHE II score of 17.70 compared to 15.33 in patients without pressure injuries; however, this difference was not statistically significant. APACHE II scores were not significantly associated with pressure injury occurrence in this study population.

In this prospective, single-group observational feasibility study, 27 conscious ICU patients receiving NPPV used a tablet-based contactless communication application for approximately 5 min. The application, developed using MediaPipe, enabled patients to select on-screen options through fingertip movements without removing the mask. articles.title: Culture and the Intensive Care Unit Team: Factors Driving Teamwork, Safety, Quality, and Well-Being.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) culture and teamwork strongly influence health care quality, patient safety, clinical outcomes, and clinician well-being. Culture shapes how multidisciplinary clinicians communicate, coordinate care, and adopt new practices. Persistent variability in ICU practices, including end-of-life care, sedation management, and mobility, often reflect differences in local culture and team dynamics. Emerging perspectives from complexity science, network science, and behavioral economics conceptualize the ICU as a complex adaptive human network in which collective behavior patterns emerge through repeated clinician interactions. Understanding ICUs through this lens may provide tools, processes, and strategies to improve health care delivery.

articles.title: Administrative Harm and Workforce Strain Indicators.
articles.abstract: The way work is structured within health care, from work environments to workloads, shapes both the workforce experience as well as job performance. Administrative harm describes the downstream effects of upstream decisions on the design of work itself, impacting workforce well-being and performance, patient care and outcomes, and organizational outcomes. The article reviews current and emerging opportunities to harness digital signals readily available within the electronic health record (EHR), including EHR use metadata and related data sources, to measure, monitor, and predict how work design (job demands and resources) affects workforce, patient, and organizational outcomes.

articles.title: Intensive Care Unit Staffing Ratios: Evidence, Experience, Economics, and Execution.
articles.abstract: The clinician-to-patient ratio is a simple construct which can be useful in strategizing for intensive care unit (ICU) staffing. Evidence is limited and inconsistent, but overall suggests such ratios may impact patient outcomes, clinician experiences, and health system economics. Importantly, however, ICU clinicians function as part of an interprofessional team, and no single staffing metric can be considered in isolation. As such, no one-size-fits-all approach to clinician-to-patient ratios exists. Yet, typical ranges are now known and decisions to operate outside of these ranges should be done with care, at least until new evidence can better guide practice.

articles.title: Moral Distress, Burnout, and the Intensive Care Unit Environment.
articles.abstract: This article examines the relationship between moral distress and burnout among intensive care unit (ICU) clinicians and argues that moral distress acts as a precursor to burnout. Moral distress arises when clinicians cannot act according to ethical obligations due to systemic constraints, leading to cumulative moral residue. In high-intensity ICU environments, this distress is driven by nonbeneficial treatment, poor communication, and resource limitations. Over time, unresolved moral distress contributes to chronic workplace stress and burnout. The authors emphasize that system-level interventions, particularly ethics consultation and organizational change, are essential to address root causes and improve clinician well-being and patient care.

articles.title: Consent for intensive care research involving adults who lack decision-making capacity: A jurisdictional analysis of Australia's fragmented framework.
articles.abstract: Critically ill adults frequently cannot consent to research because of sedation, delirium, shock or mechanical ventilation, yet safe intensive care depends on evidence generated in this population; several treatments once regarded as standard care proved harmful when finally tested in randomised trials. The ethical framework for enrolling adults who lack decision-making capacity is national-the National Health and Medical Research Council National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (2025), in effect since 23 June 2026-but legal authority for substitute consent is conferred by eight state and territory statutes that differ in terminology, in decision-maker hierarchies, in whether they address research at all, and whether they permit enrolment in an emergency. Mapping four representative study archetypes across all eight jurisdictions shows that the lawful basis for enrolling the same patient shifts with study design as much as with geography; differing statutory definitions, tribunal involvement and the transition to the 2025 National Statement produce material and avoidable inconsistency. articles.title: Kidney effects of inhaled nitric oxide in critically ill patients: from pathophysiological considerations to clinical implications.
articles.abstract: Inhaled nitric oxide is widely used as a selective pulmonary vasodilator in critical care, yet its renal effects remain controversial. While existing reviews mostly focus on indications for inhaled nitric oxide and its impact on outcomes, limited data exist on its renal effects, since it was thought to act only locally in the lungs. This review examine the clinical evidence regarding kidney outcomes associated with inhaled nitric oxide across major indications and provide an integrated mechanistic analysis of nitric oxide signaling in renal physiology and pathophysiology. Nitric oxide is produced by nitric oxide synthases using L-arginine as a substrate. It acts as a smooth muscle relaxation factor and ultimately causes vasodilation through its effect on cyclic guanosine monophosphate. Nitric oxide plays a pivotal role in renal hemodynamic regulation, glomerular filtration, tubular function, and microcirculatory homeostasis. articles.title: Short-chain fatty acid metabolism in acute lung injury and intervention strategies from traditional Chinese medicine.
articles.abstract: Acute lung injury (ALI) and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) are severe conditions associated with high mortality rates and limited treatment options. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) serve as central immunomodulatory metabolites mediate the crosstalk between the gut and lung. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), with its holistic approach, shows promise in restoring gut-lung balance and alleviating respiratory inflammation by modulating gut microbiota and SCFA metabolism. To elucidate the protective role and mechanism of SCFAs in ALI and ARDS via the gut-lung axis. Meanwhile, to evaluate the therapeutic potential of TCM in treating ALI by modulating the gut microbiota and enhancing SCFA production. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, Ovid-Embase, Web of Science, and CNKI databases (2010-2025). Keywords included "short-chain fatty acid", "gut microbes", "acute lung injury", "traditional Chinese medicine", and related terms. articles.title: Effects of Iloprost on Nitric Oxide Biomarkers in Patients With Septic Shock and Severe Endotheliopathy.
articles.abstract: Septic shock is characterized by profound endothelial dysfunction, which may involve changes in the prostacyclin and nitric oxide (NO) pathways and contribute to immune dysregulation, coagulopathy, and vascular instability. Iloprost has shown potential to modulate NO biomarkers in non-septic conditions. We investigated whether treatment with the prostacyclin analog iloprost affected plasma concentrations of the NO biomarkers ADMA, SDMA, arginine, and homoarginine in patients with septic shock and severe endotheliopathy. This preplanned sub-study of the randomized, blinded COMBAT-SHINE trial enrolled 274 adult ICU patients with septic shock and severe endotheliopathy (defined as soluble thrombomodulin (sTM) > 10 ng/mL) who had consented to the use of data. articles.title: Effect of pneumatic leg compression on post-induction hypotension in adult patients with isolated traumatic brain injury undergoing decompressive craniotomy: a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Post-induction hypotension is common after induction of general anaesthesia, and in traumatic brain injury even a brief fall in systemic pressure can compromise cerebral perfusion when autoregulation is already impaired. Pneumatic leg compression augments venous return and has reduced post-induction hypotension in obstetric and urological surgery, but has not been examined in neurotrauma patients undergoing decompressive craniotomy. In this prospective, randomised, double-blind trial, adults aged 18-65 years with isolated traumatic brain injury and radiological features of severity (midline shift ≥5 mm with basal cistern effacement) undergoing decompressive craniotomy were allocated 1:1 to a pneumatic compression device activated before induction (Group PC) or an identical device left inactive (Group NC). The primary outcome was the incidence of post-induction hypotension, defined as any recorded one-minute systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg within 20 minutes of induction. Secondary outcomes included the haemodynamic trend, fluid and vasopressor requirement, arterial blood gas changes, and device-related complications up to 72 hours. Analysis was by modified intention-to-treat.

articles.abstract: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) presents with highly variable recovery trajectories. Early identification of prognostic markers is crucial for optimizing patient management and anticipating severe complications. A systematic search of PubMed, EMBASE, and Scopus was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies reporting early clinical or electrodiagnostic predictors of functional outcomes in confirmed GBS patients were eligible. articles.abstract: Human herpesviruses (HHV) remain latent after primary infection and may reactivate during critical illness. HHV reactivation has been associated with adverse clinical outcomes, yet its pathogenic significance and optimal management remain unclear. This review summarizes the dysregulated immune mechanisms and risk factors for HHV reactivation in critical illness, treatment options, outcomes, current diagnostic challenges, and emerging precision medicine approaches. articles.abstract: Cross-kingdom dysbiosis of the gut microbiome along the gut-lung axis has emerged as a key driver of chronic and acute respiratory diseases. Beyond bacteria, the intestinal mycobiome and virome, including bacteriophages, shape mucosal immunity and metabolism through partially overlapping but non-redundant pathways. Without prophylactic measures, hypotension occurs in 60-80% of patients. Severe hypotension is associated with adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. Following intrathecal injection, a prophylactic vasopressor infusion with phenylephrine or norepinephrine should be initiated and combined with rapid crystalloid coloading. articles.title: The Pharmacologic Management of Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract: The effectiveness of pharmacologic management of cardiac arrest patients is widely debated; however, several studies published in the past 5 years have begun to clarify some of these issues. This article covers the current state of evidence for the effectiveness of the vasopressor epinephrine and the combination of vasopressin-steroids-epinephrine and antiarrhythmic medications amiodarone and lidocaine and reviews the role of other medications such as calcium, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium, and atropine in cardiac arrest care. articles.abstract: Sepsis is a major global health challenge and increasingly affects patients with complex conditions such as malignancy. Prior studies suggest higher mortality in this population, but interpretation is limited by aggregation of heterogeneous endpoints. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to clarify endpoint-specific prognostic associations between malignancy and mortality in adults with sepsis or septic shock. articles.title: Peripheral Vasopressor Administration: An Evidence-Based Risk-Benefit Analysis.
articles.abstract: Peripheral vasopressor administration has been heavily researched over the past decade as a way to quickly treat hemodynamically unstable patients. However, current evidence is diverse and limited by quality concerns, including a reliance on retrospective studies, inconsistent criteria, and bias risk. While central venous access devices (CVADs) remain the preferred route for vasopressor administration, use of the peripheral route is necessary when a CVAD is not yet present or contraindicated. Vascular access selection should be tailored to individual patient's needs. Current evidence indicates that using a protocolized approach for peripheral vasopressors appears safe and effective for low-acuity patients requiring short-term therapy (eg, less than 24 hours).

articles.abstract: Ventilation is provided to most patients during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). International guidelines emphasize the need for effective intra-arrest ventilation while acknowledging uncertainty regarding the optimal ventilation parameters. This review will discuss how new studies challenge prior beliefs on key ventilation parameters, will highlight challenges and potential solutions for high-quality ventilation and will suggest a translational research approach to advance intra-arrest ventilation. A recent observational study reported that higher ventilation rates during in-hospital cardiac arrest may be positively associated with return of spontaneous circulation, challenging common beliefs. Additionally, a pivotal observational study on bag-valve-mask ventilation during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest found that ventilation was frequently ineffective and if so, associated with reduced survival and neurological function. articles.abstract: Early randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of prone positioning (PP) in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) failed to demonstrate a survival benefit despite consistent improvements in oxygenation. Subsequent meta-analyses suggested a survival advantage in patients with severe hypoxaemia, culminating in the landmark Proning Severe ARDS Patients (PROSEVA) trial, which reported a 28-day mortality rate of 16.0% in patients with a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio <150 mmHg. Relevant clinical studies, meta-analyses, and review articles were also evaluated to provide context for the narrative review. Six RCTs were included in the main comparative analysis. articles.abstract: Perioperative infections are a common cause of morbidity in cardiac surgery. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is increasingly used as a rescue treatment for septic shock. However, data on efficacy and safety in cardiac surgery patients are limited. A scoping review of available literature aimed at identifying studies investigating the use of IVIG in patients undergoing cardiac surgery or with infective endocarditis was performed. Most studies were performed in the setting of heart transplantation, followed by nontransplant cardiac surgery and infective endocarditis. articles.title: Management of shock phenotypes after cardiac arrest: beyond cardiogenic shock.
articles.abstract: Postcardiac-arrest circulatory failure is commonly labeled cardiogenic shock, although its physiology is heterogeneous, dynamic, and frequently mixed. This review examines recent evidence and proposes a treatment-oriented framework. Hypotension, hyperlactatemia, vasopressor dependence, and myocardial dysfunction do not establish ongoing shock after cardiac arrest or identify its mechanism. Recent studies demonstrate clinically important discordance between arterial pressure, cardiac output, filling pressures, oxygen transport, metabolic recovery, and prognosis. Four primary hemodynamic phenotypes are proposed: vasoplegic-inflammatory shock; myocardial dysfunction and low-flow shock; hypovolemia; and right ventricular and pulmonary vascular dysfunction. Mixed shock is an overlap group, whereas reversible metabolic pseudoshock describes arrest-related hyperlactatemia that resolves without persistent hemodynamic compromise. articles.abstract: Albumin preparations are the most common colloids used in critically ill patients worldwide. This review is to provide the physiological rationale and evidence for benefits and harms in different clinical settings. There is a strong physiological rationale for intravenous albumin administration in critically ill patients. Iso-oncotic and hyperoncotic albumin have both been used for volume resuscitation and to maintain effective plasma volume at an optimal fluid balance. articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and severe complication in critically ill patients, associated with high morbidity and mortality. Renal replacement therapy (RRT) is a vital life-support modality for critically ill patients with AKI. However, there remains a lack of unified clinical standards for core issues including the timing of RRT initiation, treatment modality, anticoagulation strategy, and weaning from RRT. In response, the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine organized a multidisciplinary expert panel to develop the "Clinical practice guideline for RRT in critically ill patients with AKI (2026 edition)" in accordance with the GRADE approach for grading evidence quality. articles.abstract: Carbapenemase-producing Gram-negative bacteria are among the most challenging pathogens encountered in contemporary infectious diseases and critical care practice. Although antimicrobial susceptibility testing remains the cornerstone of laboratory diagnosis, reliance on the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) in isolation is insufficient to predict clinical outcome. From an EMS perspective, requirements are defined for activation, prenotification, team structure, handover, overload management and feedback. Written activation and allocation criteria are required that are applicable in the prehospital setting and agreed upon by hospitals, emergency dispatch centres and EMS providers. articles.abstract: Malnutrition and accelerated muscle wasting are frequent during critical illness and make nutritional support a central component of ICU care. Nutritional support is therefore central to ICU care, but its optimal timing, route, dose, and composition remain debated. Recent randomized trials have challenged the traditional objective of early full feeding and shifted practice toward progressive, phase-adapted, and tolerance-based nutrition. This narrative review compares current international guidelines for nutritional support in critically ill adults. articles.abstract: Survivorship of critical illness has increased, shifting attention toward recovery and long-term outcomes. Post-ICU nutrition is emerging as a clinically relevant, yet underperforming contributor to functional recovery and quality of life.
